question: What is physiotherapy?
answer: Physiotherapy (also called physical therapy) is the use of exercise, manual treatment, and education to restore movement and reduce pain. It is non-surgical and drug-free. A physiotherapist assesses how your joints, muscles, and nerves are working, finds the cause of the problem, and gives you a tailored plan. Common reasons people see us include back and neck pain, sports injuries, post-surgery rehab, stroke recovery, and conditions such as arthritis or sciatica.

question: What does a physiotherapist do?
answer: A physiotherapist is a healthcare professional trained to evaluate movement problems and treat them with exercise, manual therapy (hands-on techniques), and education. They build a personalised programme for you, teach you home exercises, track your progress, and refer you on if imaging or medical review is needed. They do not prescribe medicines.

question: What conditions can physiotherapy help with?
answer: Physiotherapy helps with a wide range of issues: muscle and joint pain (back, neck, knee, shoulder), sports injuries, post-fracture or post-surgery recovery, sciatica, frozen shoulder, plantar fasciitis, arthritis, balance and falls in older adults, and rehab after a stroke or heart attack. If your problem is mostly mechanical (worse with movement, better with rest or specific positions), physiotherapy is usually the first-line treatment.

question: How often should I do my home exercises?
answer: Most home exercise programmes work best when done once or twice a day, 4 to 5 days a week. Stick to the reps and sets your physiotherapist gave you and stop if you feel sharp pain. Consistency matters more than intensity, especially in the first two weeks.

question: Is it normal to feel sore after a session?
answer: Mild soreness for 24 to 48 hours after a session is normal, especially in the first few weeks. Sharp pain, swelling that does not settle, or pain that wakes you at night is not. Contact your physiotherapist if soreness is severe or lasts more than 3 days.

question: How many physiotherapy sessions will I need?
answer: It depends on the condition. Most patients see meaningful change within 6 to 12 sessions. Acute injuries may need fewer, chronic problems often need more. Your physiotherapist will review your progress every 4 to 6 sessions and adjust the plan.

question: When can I return to running after an injury?
answer: Generally when you can walk briskly without pain, hop on the affected leg ten times, and complete your prescribed strength exercises pain-free. Start with a walk-jog programme of 1 minute jog and 2 minutes walk. Increase gradually by no more than 10% per week.

question: What should I bring to my first physiotherapy session?
answer: Bring any referral letter, recent scan or X-ray reports, a list of current medicines, and comfortable clothing you can move in. Loose shorts or leggings and a t-shirt work best. Allow 45 to 60 minutes for the first visit.

question: What should I wear to a physiotherapy session?
answer: Wear loose, comfortable clothing that allows free movement and access to the area we are treating. Shorts for knee or hip work, a t-shirt or vest for shoulder work. Bring trainers if we are doing balance or running drills. Avoid jeans.

question: What is the difference between heat and ice for an injury?
answer: Ice (cold therapy) is for new injuries in the first 48 to 72 hours to reduce swelling and pain. Heat is for stiff, tight muscles and chronic aches to relax tissue and improve blood flow. If unsure, ice fresh injuries and heat older problems.

question: How long should I ice an injury?
answer: Apply ice for 15 to 20 minutes at a time, with at least an hour between sessions, for the first 48 to 72 hours. Use a thin towel between the ice pack and your skin to prevent ice burn. Do not sleep on an ice pack.

question: Is bed rest good for back pain?
answer: No. Modern evidence shows long bed rest delays recovery and weakens muscles. Stay as active as the pain allows, walk regularly, and avoid lying down for more than a few hours. Most acute back pain settles within 6 weeks with gentle movement.

question: What is sciatica?
answer: Sciatica is pain that radiates down the back of the leg, usually from irritation of the sciatic nerve in the lower back. Common causes are a disc bulge or tight muscles pressing on the nerve. Most cases improve within 6 to 12 weeks with exercise and posture work.

question: Can I exercise with a sore shoulder?
answer: Yes, gentle exercise is usually safe and helpful. Avoid lifting overhead, heavy weights, or any movement that causes sharp pain. Pendulum swings, scapular squeezes, and gentle stretches are good starting points. Stop if pain becomes worse than mild.

question: How do I prevent back pain when working at a desk?
answer: Sit with feet flat, hips slightly above knees, and screen at eye level. Stand up every 30 to 45 minutes for one minute, even if only to walk to the kitchen. Strengthen your core with simple exercises a few times a week. Avoid slouching for long periods.

question: What is dry needling?
answer: Dry needling uses thin acupuncture-style needles inserted into tight muscle trigger points to release tension. It is different from acupuncture, which is based on traditional Chinese medicine. Most patients feel a brief ache during and slight soreness for a day after.

question: What is TENS therapy?
answer: TENS (transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation) sends a gentle electrical current through pads on the skin to reduce pain by stimulating large nerve fibres. It is safe for most adults and can be used at home. Avoid TENS over the heart, on broken skin, or if you have a pacemaker.

question: What is ultrasound therapy?
answer: Therapeutic ultrasound uses high-frequency sound waves to warm deep tissue and promote healing. Sessions last 5 to 10 minutes and you usually feel a mild warmth. Evidence shows it helps tendinitis and some soft-tissue injuries, especially in combination with exercise.

question: Can I stretch every day?
answer: Yes. Daily gentle stretching keeps joints mobile and muscles supple. Hold each stretch 20 to 30 seconds and avoid bouncing. Stretch to mild tension, not pain. Warm up with a few minutes of walking first to reduce the risk of strain.

question: Why does my knee click or pop?
answer: Knees can click for many reasons: gas bubbles releasing, tendons crossing over bone, or mild cartilage roughness. Clicks without pain or swelling are usually not a problem. See a physiotherapist if clicking is painful, came after an injury, or is associated with a feeling that the knee gives way.

question: Is cracking my knuckles or back harmful?
answer: Cracking joints by stretching or moving is generally safe and does not cause arthritis. The sound is a small gas bubble forming in the joint fluid. Forceful manipulation of the neck or back without training can occasionally cause harm, so leave that to a qualified professional.

question: What is the best sleep position for back pain?
answer: Lying on your back with a pillow under your knees, or on your side with a pillow between your knees, takes pressure off the lower back. Sleeping on the stomach can strain the neck and lower back. A medium-firm mattress suits most people.

question: How do I set up my home work desk?
answer: Top of the screen at eye level, elbows bent at 90 degrees when typing, feet flat on the floor, lower back supported. Use an external keyboard and mouse if working from a laptop. A separate chair with adjustable height is worth the investment.

question: Can I drive home after my physiotherapy session?
answer: Yes, for most sessions. You may feel a little stiff or sore but driving is safe. After dry needling, deep tissue work, or manipulation you may feel slightly drowsy or sore, so wait 15 to 30 minutes before driving if needed.

question: How long until I see results from physiotherapy?
answer: Most patients notice some improvement within 2 to 4 sessions. Tissue healing and strength gains take 6 to 12 weeks. If you see no change after 4 to 6 sessions, the plan is reviewed and may be adjusted. Stick with your home exercises between visits.

question: Does physiotherapy hurt?
answer: Some techniques cause mild, brief discomfort, especially deep tissue release, dry needling, or stretching tight joints. Sharp pain is not acceptable and we will adjust the technique. Most exercises and treatments should feel like effort, not pain.

question: What is a frozen shoulder?
answer: Frozen shoulder, or adhesive capsulitis, is gradual stiffness and pain in the shoulder joint over months. It goes through three phases: freezing (painful), frozen (stiff), and thawing (gradual recovery). Full recovery can take 12 to 18 months and is helped by stretching, mobilisation, and sometimes a steroid injection.

question: Can I do physiotherapy at home without going to a clinic?
answer: For mild aches and stiffness, a home programme can be enough if you follow it correctly. For pain that limits daily life, comes after an injury, or includes numbness, get assessed first. A clinician can rule out red flags and tailor exercises to your body.

question: What is core stability?
answer: Core stability is the ability of the deep abdominal, back, and pelvic muscles to keep the spine well supported during movement. Strong core muscles reduce back pain, improve posture, and help athletic performance. Plank, dead-bug, and bird-dog exercises are good starting points.

question: How do I prevent running injuries?
answer: Increase weekly mileage by no more than 10%. Strengthen calves, glutes, and hamstrings twice a week. Replace shoes every 600 to 800 km. Warm up with 5 minutes of brisk walking and listen to early pain signs rather than running through them.

question: Should I exercise when I have a cold or flu?
answer: If symptoms are above the neck (runny nose, sore throat) and you feel well, light exercise is fine. If you have a fever, body aches, or chest symptoms, rest and recover. Resume gently with half your usual workload for the first few sessions back.

question: What is the best shoe for plantar fasciitis?
answer: Look for shoes with firm heel support, a slight cushion, and a stiff midsole. Avoid completely flat shoes and unsupportive sandals. Off-the-shelf gel heel cups and arch supports help many people. Stretch the calves and roll a tennis ball under the arch daily.

question: When should I see a doctor instead of a physiotherapist?
answer: See a doctor if you have unexplained weight loss, fever, severe night pain, loss of bladder or bowel control, sudden weakness, or numbness in the groin or both legs. These can be signs that need urgent medical assessment. Physiotherapists also refer onward if these signs appear.

question: Should I use heat or ice on my injury?
answer: Use ice for the first 48 hours after a fresh injury - 15 minutes at a time, wrapped in a cloth - to reduce swelling. Use heat for stiff or chronic pain to relax muscles before exercises. If swelling is severe or pain is sharp and increasing, do not heat; book a review instead.

question: Is bed rest okay for back pain?
answer: More than 1-2 days of bed rest usually makes back pain worse. Stay as active as you can: walk, change positions often, and gently move the spine. Pain medication for the first 2-3 days plus a graded exercise plan gives the best results for most acute back pain.

question: How long should a stretch be held?
answer: For flexibility, hold each static stretch for 20-30 seconds and repeat 2-3 times per side. Do not bounce. You should feel a gentle pull, not pain. Warm up with light activity first; stretching cold muscles can cause strains.

question: How do I prevent back pain at my desk?
answer: Set the chair so feet are flat and hips are slightly higher than knees. Top of the monitor at eye level. Keep the keyboard close so elbows are at 90 degrees. Stand up and walk for 1-2 minutes every 30-40 minutes. A small lumbar roll can help maintain the natural curve of the lower back.

question: Why does my knee click during exercises?
answer: Painless clicking is common and is usually fluid or tendons moving over bony surfaces. Clicking with pain, locking, or giving way needs review. Keep doing your exercises as long as they are pain-free and tell your physiotherapist at the next session.

question: What is the best sleep position for lower back pain?
answer: Sleep on your back with a pillow under the knees, or on your side with a pillow between the knees. Avoid sleeping on your stomach as it strains the lower back and neck. A medium-firm mattress is generally best.

question: What is plantar fasciitis and what shoes help?
answer: Plantar fasciitis is inflammation of the band of tissue under the foot, often felt as sharp heel pain in the morning. Shoes with cushioned heels, arch support, and a small heel-to-toe drop help most. Avoid walking barefoot on hard floors and add calf and plantar fascia stretches.

question: How long does a physio session usually last?
answer: A first appointment usually takes 45-60 minutes (history, assessment, initial treatment, and home plan). Follow-up sessions are 30-45 minutes. Tell us if you need a longer slot for complex pain or post-surgical work.

question: Should I do exercises through pain?
answer: Some discomfort up to about 4 out of 10 is acceptable and may be necessary to make progress. Pain above that level or sharp pain means stop and contact us. The pain should settle within 24 hours of exercise; if it lingers, the load was too high.

question: Can physio help vertigo?
answer: Yes - vestibular physiotherapy uses head-position manoeuvres (such as Epley for BPPV) and gaze-stabilisation exercises. Most patients with positional vertigo improve in 1-3 sessions. Vertigo with hearing loss, neurological signs, or severe imbalance needs medical review first.

question: What is a TENS machine and does it work?
answer: TENS (transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation) delivers tiny electrical pulses through skin pads to reduce pain. Evidence is moderate for short-term relief in chronic low back, knee, and labour pain. It is safe for most people; avoid it over a pacemaker, broken skin, or the front of the neck.

question: Should I use a back brace for my low back pain?
answer: Routine use of a lumbar brace for non-specific back pain is not recommended - it tends to weaken the core muscles. Short-term use during a flare-up or heavy lifting can help. The real long-term fix is graded exercise and movement, which we will plan together.

question: What is the difference between sprain and strain?
answer: A sprain is an injury to a ligament (the tough band connecting two bones), commonly the ankle or knee. A strain is an injury to a muscle or tendon, commonly the hamstring or lower back. Both heal with the PEACE & LOVE protocol - Protection, Elevation, Avoid anti-inflammatories early, Compression, Education, then Load, Optimism, Vascularisation, Exercise.

question: How much walking should I do each day?
answer: Aim for 30-60 minutes of brisk walking on most days. Break it into 10-minute blocks if continuous walking is hard. Start with what feels comfortable and add 5-10 minutes per week. A simple step counter (8,000-10,000 steps a day for most adults) is a good motivator.

question: My ankle gives way often - what should I do?
answer: Recurrent giving-way is usually because the ligaments and the small balance receptors around the ankle have not retrained after the original sprain. A balance programme (single-leg stand, wobble board, jumps and lands), heel-raises, and lateral hops over 6-8 weeks fixes this in most people.

question: Are deep tissue massages safe during pregnancy?
answer: Pregnancy massage is safe from the second trimester when delivered by a trained therapist in a side-lying position. Avoid deep abdominal pressure, heat, and lying flat on the back. Tell your physiotherapist if you have any pregnancy complications such as placenta praevia.

question: What is the rotator cuff and how do you injure it?
answer: The rotator cuff is a group of four small muscles (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis) that hold the ball of the shoulder in the socket and lift the arm. It is injured by repeated overhead work, a fall onto an outstretched hand, or gradual age-related wear. Most tears improve with a structured exercise programme - surgery is reserved for full-thickness tears with persistent weakness.

question: Can physiotherapy help with chronic neck pain at the computer?
answer: Yes. Most desk-related neck pain is a mix of fatigued deep neck flexors, tight upper trapezius, and a forward-head posture. We assess your workstation, give you 5-minute mobility breaks (chin tucks, scapular squeezes, thoracic extensions), and add a graded strength programme. Most people improve within 6-8 weeks.

question: Should I exercise during a migraine?
answer: During the acute headache, rest in a quiet dark room. Between attacks, regular aerobic exercise (150 minutes a week of brisk walking, swimming or cycling) reduces migraine frequency by about a third. Avoid sudden very intense effort if it triggers attacks for you.

question: What is the role of dry land exercises before knee surgery?
answer: Prehabilitation - strength and range-of-motion exercises in the 4-6 weeks before knee replacement - speeds up recovery, reduces post-op pain, and shortens hospital stay. Focus on quadriceps strength, hip abduction, and learning to walk with crutches before the operation.

question: How is an ACL injury managed without surgery?
answer: Partial ACL tears and complete tears in non-athletes are often managed with structured rehab over 3-6 months: quadriceps strengthening, hamstring co-contraction, balance and proprioception drills, plus a progressive return-to-running programme. Surgery is offered for younger athletes, repeated giving-way, or combined ligament injuries.

question: What are shin splints and how do you treat them?
answer: Shin splints (medial tibial stress syndrome) are pain along the inner edge of the shin caused by overuse, often during running. Treatment is reduce the running volume by 50%, ice after activity, calf and tibialis posterior strengthening, and supportive shoes. Pain that persists for more than 4 weeks should be reviewed to exclude a stress fracture.

question: What is tennis elbow and how do I fix it?
answer: Tennis elbow (lateral epicondylitis) is pain on the outside of the elbow from overuse of the wrist extensor tendons - common in racket sports, gym work, and desk jobs. Eccentric wrist exercises (3 sets of 15, twice a day) are the most evidence-based fix; takes 6-12 weeks to feel significant improvement.

question: What is golfer's elbow?
answer: Golfer's elbow (medial epicondylitis) is the inside-of-the-elbow version of tennis elbow, affecting the wrist flexor tendons. It is common in golf, climbing, and forceful gripping work. Eccentric wrist-flexor exercises plus a forearm strap usually resolve it in 8-12 weeks.

question: What is hydrotherapy and when do you use it?
answer: Hydrotherapy is supervised exercise in a warm pool. The buoyancy unloads painful joints and resistance to movement is gentle, making it ideal for early post-op rehab, severe osteoarthritis, fibromyalgia, and some neurological conditions. Sessions are 30-45 minutes and usually 1-2 per week alongside dry-land work.

question: What is a postural assessment?
answer: A postural assessment looks at how you stand, sit, and move to identify imbalances that contribute to pain. We check spinal curves, shoulder symmetry, pelvic tilt, foot arch, and how your muscles activate during simple movements. It guides individualised stretches, strength work, and ergonomic advice.

question: Can physiotherapy help with breathing problems?
answer: Yes - pulmonary physiotherapy helps with COPD, asthma, post-COVID breathlessness, and pre/post chest-surgery recovery. We teach diaphragmatic breathing, pursed-lip breathing, the active cycle of breathing techniques, and inspiratory muscle training. Sessions are 30-45 minutes.

question: What is the recovery timeline after a meniscus repair?
answer: After arthroscopic meniscus repair you are usually on crutches for 4-6 weeks with a brace limiting knee flexion. Return to running is at 12-16 weeks and to contact sport at 4-6 months. A meniscectomy (removing torn tissue rather than repairing it) recovers faster - 2-4 weeks for daily activity.

question: How is geriatric balance training done?
answer: We use the Tinetti and Berg Balance Scale to grade fall risk, then progress from sit-to-stand drills to single-leg stance, tandem walking, foam-surface exercises, and dual-task drills (walking while counting). A 12-week programme typically halves the fall rate in community-dwelling older adults.

question: What is the difference between manual therapy and chiropractic?
answer: Manual therapy by a physiotherapist uses joint mobilisation, soft-tissue release, and muscle energy techniques alongside a structured exercise programme. Chiropractors typically use higher-velocity spinal manipulation. Both can help short-term back and neck pain; physiotherapy adds the long-term exercise plan that prevents relapse.

question: Can I exercise with osteoarthritis?
answer: Yes - exercise is the best non-drug treatment for osteoarthritis. Low-impact aerobic work (walking, cycling, swimming), targeted strengthening of muscles around the affected joint, and gentle range-of-motion work reduce pain and slow progression. Avoid prolonged high-impact loading on a flared joint.

question: What is gait analysis and when do I need it?
answer: Gait analysis observes how you walk or run - heel-strike, push-off, hip control, arm swing - to identify mechanics that cause pain or injury. We use video review and pressure mats. It is useful for recurrent running injuries, post-stroke walking difficulty, and to fit orthotics correctly.

question: What is hand therapy?
answer: Hand therapy is specialist physiotherapy for fingers, hand, wrist, and elbow injuries: fractures, tendon repairs, nerve injuries, arthritis, and post-burn rehab. It includes custom splinting, scar massage, range-of-motion exercises, and dexterity drills. Sessions are typically 30 minutes.

question: My child has been diagnosed with flat feet - should I be worried?
answer: Most children have flat feet up to age 6 because the arch develops slowly. Painless flexible flat feet need no treatment. Rigid flat feet, or pain, fatigue with walking, or asymmetric arches, should be reviewed - supportive shoes, calf stretches, and a short course of supervised exercises usually help.

question: How do I return to running after a calf strain?
answer: Once you can heel-raise on the injured leg 30 times without pain and walk briskly for 30 minutes pain-free, start a walk-jog progression: 1 minute jog, 2 minutes walk, 5 cycles, three times a week. Increase total running time by no more than 10% per week, and re-injure if you skip the strength work first.
